title: The daily banis, in the code
hookLine: the code lists the morning, evening and night banis

lines: THE DAY HAS MARKS IN IT.
cards: On an old sailing ship, a bell was struck at set times through the day and night, so everyone aboard knew where the day stood without looking for a clock. The day had marks in it, and the marks held the crew together.
The code gives the Sikh day its marks too: which prayers are said, and when. Morning, evening, night.

teach.b: The daily set is called nitnem, the daily rule. Each piece in it is a bani, a composition of the Gurus. In paraphrase, here's the code's list.
In the morning: Japji Sahib, the Jaap Sahib, and the Ten Swayyas, the ones that begin with the words sravag sudh. In the evening: Sodar Rehras, a gathering of hymns read as the day goes down.
At night, before sleep: Sohila. Part of this list came up a few days ago, from the Tenth Guru's side. Now look at all of it, and at who is speaking.

teach.h: THE FIRST GURU AND THE TENTH TOGETHER.
teach.b: Japji Sahib is Guru Nanak's, the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib. The Jaap Sahib and the Swayyas are the Tenth Guru's, the writings of the last few weeks.
So the morning opens with the first Guru and the Tenth side by side, the beginning of the line and its end, before breakfast. Then the shape.
Three doors in the day: one as it starts, one as it turns toward dark, one as it closes. Nobody has to decide each day whether to pray or what to say. The code has already set the table.

teach.h: A SHARED FLOOR, NOT A CEILING.
teach.b: The code's list is a shared floor, not a ceiling. Some Sikh communities and schools add more banis to the morning, and families keep their own additions.
The code names what Sikhs agree on together. So the stretch that began with the Tenth Guru's own writings ends with two of them set into a daily timetable. They aren't only studied.
They're said aloud, morning after morning.

how: Sikhs who keep nitnem recite the morning banis after waking, Rehras in the evening and Sohila before sleep, often from a gutka or from memory; some communities add further banis to the morning.

o: the set prayers said at morning, evening and night
hymns sung only at weddings and festivals
the weekly readings given out at a gurdwara

games.q: the code's nitnem: tap the pairs.

s: the code names Japji Sahib for the morning
Japji Sahib, Jaap Sahib and the Swayyas that begin sravag sudh.
the code's nitnem has nothing for the night
Sohila is said at night, before sleep.
every community reads exactly the code's list and no more
the code's list is a shared floor. some communities and families add more to the morning.

games.q: the day was long and the light is going. which bani does the code name for this hour?
games.why: Rehras is the evening bani. Japji opens the morning, and Sohila waits for the moment before sleep.

practice: Walk through yesterday in your mind, waking, midday, evening, the moment before sleep, and see where the doors were, a moment of quiet, a word of thanks, a prayer or nothing at all, without judging it.
Then choose one door and picture what you'd like to find there, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru with each breath.

wordCard.voice: The daily banis. The code's nitnem: Japji, Jaap and the Swayyas at morning, Rehras at evening, Sohila at night. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the daily rule, the set banis said each day.

carryVoice: Your line: the code's nitnem. Three doors, and the table already set. That's today, done.
